Texas had a total population of about **28,635,442** in the ACS 2020 5-year release. I got this by adding up all 18,638 Texas block groups.

- This is a sample-based estimate averaged over 2016–2020. It isn't a count from a single year, and it isn't the 2020 Decennial Census count.
- I took "Texas" to mean the state. If you meant Texas County, Missouri, or Texas County, Oklahoma, I can look up either one.

Source: ACS 2020 5-year (2016-2020), B01003 (Total population), field B01003e1, summed over block groups.

The five states with the highest share of residents aged 65 and over are Maine, Florida, West Virginia, Vermont and Delaware. These figures come from the 2020 ACS 5-year release, which covers 2016–2020.

| Rank | State | Total population | Aged 65+ | Share 65+ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Maine | 1,340,825 | 276,567 | 20.6% |
| 2 | Florida | 21,216,924 | 4,347,912 | 20.5% |
| 3 | West Virginia | 1,807,426 | 360,246 | 19.9% |
| 4 | Vermont | 624,340 | 120,872 | 19.4% |
| 5 | Delaware | 967,679 | 182,024 | 18.8% |

**Notes:**
- **Puerto Rico** isn't a state, but it's in the dataset. At 20.5% it would rank between Florida and West Virginia.
- **Close gaps:** Maine and Florida differ by only 0.1 points, and Montana (18.7%) is just behind Delaware. These are survey estimates with sampling error, so rankings this close aren't certain.
- **Just outside the top five:** Montana (18.7%), Hawaii (18.4%), Pennsylvania (18.3%) and New Hampshire (18.1%).

Source: ACS 2020 5-year (2016–2020), B01001 (Sex by Age). The 65+ count is male fields B01001e20–e25 plus female fields B01001e44–e49, divided by total population B01001e1, all summed over block groups.

I estimate King County's median household income at about **$99,300** (in 2020 dollars), using the ACS 2020 5-year release (2016–2020). This is my own estimate, not an official Census figure. The dataset only has medians for individual block groups, and you can't get a county median by averaging those.

**How I estimated it**
- I added up the household income bracket counts from table B19001 across all of King County's block groups. That comes to 900,061 households.
- The middle household is number 450,031. That household falls in the **$75,000–$99,999** bracket: 346,486 households earn less than $75,000, and 453,017 earn less than $100,000.
- I then estimated the median's position within that bracket, assuming incomes are spread evenly across it (linear interpolation). That gives about $99,300, which is near the top of the bracket.

**Related figure:** the **mean** household income is about **$134,707**. That's total household income ($121.2 billion) divided by 900,061 households. The mean is much higher than the median because of the top incomes: 170,181 households (18.9%) earn $200,000 or more.

All of these numbers come from survey samples, so they carry sampling error.

Source: ACS 2020 5-year (2016–2020), B19001 (Household income, fields B19001e1–e17) and B19025 (Aggregate household income, field B19025e1), summed over King County block groups (GEOID prefix 53033).

I can't tell you how California has changed since 2010 from this dataset. It only has two ACS 5-year releases: 2019 (survey years 2015–2019) and 2020 (survey years 2016–2020). There's no 2010 data in it, so I can't measure a change over the decade.

The closest I can give you is a comparison of those two releases:

| Release | Survey years | California population |
|---|---|---|
| ACS 2019 5-year | 2015–2019 | 39,283,497 |
| ACS 2020 5-year | 2016–2020 | 39,346,023 |
| **Difference** | | **+62,526 (+0.2%)** |

**This isn't a real year-over-year change.** The two releases share four of their five survey years (2016–2019). So the difference mostly reflects swapping 2015 out for 2020, plus sampling error. The Census Bureau advises comparing only 5-year periods that don't overlap, and this dataset doesn't have any.

For a true 2010-to-present trend, the Census Bureau's decennial counts (2010 and 2020) or its annual population estimates would be the right sources. Neither is in this dataset.

Florida's estimated population went up by **315,288 people (about 1.5%)**, from 20,901,636 in the 2019 release to 21,216,924 in the 2020 release.

| ACS 5-year release | Years covered | Florida population |
|---|---|---|
| 2019 | 2015–2019 | 20,901,636 |
| 2020 | 2016–2020 | 21,216,924 |
| **Change** | | **+315,288 (+1.5%)** |

**This is not a change from 2019 to 2020.** Each figure is an average over five years of surveys, and the two releases share four of those years (2016–2019). So the gap really reflects swapping out 2015 for 2020. It shows the general direction but shouldn't be read as growth in a single year. The Census Bureau advises comparing 5-year periods that don't overlap, and this dataset only has these two releases. Both figures are survey estimates, so they also carry sampling error.

Source: ACS 2019 5-year (2015–2019) and ACS 2020 5-year (2016–2020), B01003 (Total population), field B01003e1, summed over Florida block groups (GEOID prefix 12).

In Cook County, IL, the share of households earning under $25,000 fell from **20.3%** in the 2019 release to **19.2%** in the 2020 release. That's a drop of about 1.1 percentage points, or about 18,552 fewer households.

| Release | Total households | Households under $25,000 | Share |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2019 (2015–2019) | 1,972,108 | 401,095 | 20.3% |
| 2020 (2016–2020) | 1,991,474 | 382,543 | 19.2% |

**Why this isn't a clean one-year change:**
- **Overlapping years:** The two 5-year releases share four of their five survey years (2016–2019). The difference really reflects swapping 2015 out for 2020, not change from 2019 to 2020. The Census Bureau advises comparing periods that don't overlap.
- **Different dollars:** Each release states income in its own inflation-adjusted dollars ("2019 dollars" vs "2020 dollars"). So the $25,000 line is slightly different in real terms between the two releases.
- **Sampling error:** These are survey estimates and carry sampling error, so a small change like this should be read with caution.

Source: ACS 2019 5-year (2015–2019) and ACS 2020 5-year (2016–2020), B19001 (Household income in the past 12 months). Fields B19001e1 (total) and B19001e2–e5 (under $10,000 through $20,000–$24,999), summed over Cook County block groups (GEOID prefix 17031).

The table below has the population and an estimated median household income for all 50 states, DC and Puerto Rico (52 rows), sorted by population. I used the 2020 release (2016–2020).

**Population:**
- California is the largest at 39,346,023, then Texas (28,635,442) and Florida (21,216,924).
- Wyoming is the smallest state at 581,348. Vermont (624,340) and DC (701,974) are also among the smallest.

**Estimated median household income (in 2020 dollars):**
- **Highest:** DC (about $91,700), Maryland (about $87,700), New Jersey (about $86,000) and Massachusetts (about $85,000).
- **Lowest states:** Mississippi (about $46,600), West Virginia (about $48,100) and Arkansas (about $49,500).
- **Puerto Rico** is much lower than any state, at about $21,100.

**How I got the income figures:** The dataset only has median incomes for small neighbourhood-sized areas (block groups), not for whole states, so it can't give an exact state median. Instead, I added up each state's households in each income bracket and estimated where the middle household falls within its bracket. These are estimates and may differ from official state medians. All figures carry sampling error.

Source: ACS 2020 5-year (2016–2020). Population from B01003 (Total population), field B01003e1. Household counts and income brackets from B19001 (Household Income), fields B19001e1–e17. All summed over block groups by state, with the median interpolated from the brackets.
